subtype: Approach: sets triggers for switching to plan B [Action]
passage:
Trisha was organising the craft fair for women weavers in Mahuva, a small town near the coast, and she had booked the big community hall, which held two hundred. But last year only forty people had come, and the empty hall had felt sad.
This time, three weeks before, she sat in the panchayat office with her friend Bidisha and wrote a rule. "If fewer than sixty weavers and buyers confirm by Friday at six, we move to the smaller school hall." She told the school headmaster the same day, and he agreed to keep it free.
"Why decide now?" Bidisha asked.
"Because on the day I'll be panicking and want to hope for the best," Trisha said.
On Friday at six, the count was fifty-one. Trisha didn't argue with herself. She called the school and the community hall, and sent a message to all fifty-one: new venue, same time.
The school hall was full and lively.

qa.q: How many confirmations were there on Friday at six?
Why did Trisha want to set the rule three weeks early?
qa.a: She worried she would panic on the day and just hope for the best, so she wanted the decision made calmly in advance.

qa.q: What else could Trisha set a trigger for, and why?
qa.a: She could set a rule for bad weather, such as moving stalls indoors if rain is forecast, so another choice isn't made in a rush.

qa.q: How might the weavers experience the smaller hall?
qa.a: They may feel more encouraged, since a full, lively hall feels better than the sad, empty one of last year.

grounding: It shows an organiser deciding in advance that if fewer than sixty confirm by Friday, she will move to the smaller hall, rather than deciding under pressure on the day.

subtype: Approach: sets triggers for switching to plan B [Action]
passage:
Ulla was organising the neighbourhood winter supper in Aarhus. The big church hall seated a hundred and twenty and cost four times as much as the library's meeting room, which seated seventy.
Her friend Dalia said, "Just book the big one. People always come."
"Last year they didn't," Ulla said. "Half the tables were empty." She opened her laptop. "So here's the rule. If fewer than sixty people have signed up by Friday noon, we move to the library room. If it's sixty or more, we keep the hall."
She told the library to hold the room until Friday afternoon and wrote the rule at the top of the sign-up sheet so the volunteers knew too.
Friday at noon, the sheet showed fifty-four names. Ulla sent one email: "We'll be cosy this year. Library, 6 p.m."
Dalia replied with a thumbs up. That evening, the library room was warm and full.

qa.q: How many names were on the sheet on Friday at noon?
How might Ulla have felt at noon on Friday when the count came in?
qa.a: She probably felt calm and settled, because the decision was already made by her rule.

qa.q: What else could Ulla do if sign-ups jump after the switch?
qa.a: She could set a second rule, such as a waiting list over seventy, so the small room doesn't get overcrowded.

qa.q: How might Dalia see Ulla's rule?
qa.a: Dalia first wanted to book the big hall, but seems happy with the outcome, sending a thumbs up.

grounding: It shows an organiser setting a Friday trigger of sixty sign-ups for switching to a smaller room, instead of deciding under pressure on the day.
